articles.title: Mexico Advances Circular Economy Strategy for Sargassum
articles.author: Mexico Business News
articles.content:
Mexico is advancing a science-based, multi-stakeholder strategy to manage and industrialize sargassum through initiatives such as Caribe Circular, supported by research from IMIPAS and monitoring systems from UNAM. The effort seeks to integrate the macroalgae into regulated value chains while addressing environmental risks to coastal ecosystems and tourism, a key economic sector. This development is shaping investment opportunities and regulatory frameworks in the blue economy, with implications for hospitality, manufacturing, and environmental management industries across the Mexican Caribbean.
___________________________________________________________________________________________
Mexico is advancing a scientific and industrial strategy to turn sargassum from an environmental threat into an economic resource. Through the Caribe Circular initiative, research, monitoring, and cross-sector collaboration aim to enable sustainable management, new value chains, and regional replication across the Caribbean.
The Mexican Institute for Sustainable Fisheries and Aquaculture Research has joined the Caribe Circular initiative, contributing scientific knowledge on sargassum with the aim of achieving its sustainable management and industrial use.
The Caribe Circular project, which brings together stakeholders from the hotel and restaurant sectors, seeks to identify profitable uses for sargassum, such as converting it into raw material for products like plates, utensils, bioplastics, and packaging materials, thereby promoting a circular economy in the region.
Through specialized studies, IMIPAS has documented the scale of the phenomenon as well as its biological, oceanographic, and ecological characteristics. In May 2025, with funding from the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB), the institute carried out a first comprehensive assessment of pelagic sargassum in the Mexican Caribbean’s Exclusive Economic Zone. The study revealed that the actual amount of sargassum in open waters could be nearly three times higher than previously estimated. This finding reshapes the magnitude of the challenge while opening the door to its sustainable use.
The scientific expedition also found that sargassum rafts function as floating ecosystems hosting remarkable biodiversity. More than 870 organisms per kilogram of sargassum were documented. This has direct implications for management: indiscriminate removal can eliminate critical habitats for fishery species, meaning that any utilization strategy must incorporate ecological criteria and responsible management protocols.
The expedition further revealed that the content of elements such as phosphorus varies depending on species and location. In general terms, sargassum from the Mexican Caribbean contains around 20% carbon, 0.35–0.42% nitrogen, and in some cases high levels of phosphorus. This suggests that strategic harvesting could maximize its value as an agricultural input.
Additionally, sargassum is rich in alginates and fucoidans, polysaccharides used in the food, pharmaceutical, and cosmetics industries. Its high carbon content also makes it a candidate for biogas, biochar, and other circular economy and carbon capture solutions. This information is key for decision-making and for designing strategies to mitigate the impact of this macroalgae on coastal ecosystems, tourism activity, and local communities.
Thanks to this type of research, sargassum is increasingly being reevaluated as a resource. In Mexico, its inclusion in the National Fisheries Charter represents an important step toward recognizing its potential within the fisheries sector and advancing regulated use. However, its management still entails costs of approximately US$150 million for both authorities and companies.
In this context, and with the aim of maintaining continuous monitoring of sargassum blooms, the National Laboratory for Earth Observation at the UNAM has deployed a surveillance system to prevent the algae from reaching reefs and beaches, where ecological and economic impacts are immediate. Last year alone, approximately 96,000t of sargassum were collected in Quintana Roo, a figure that, according to estimates, may increase this season.
When sargassum accumulates and decomposes along the coast, it creates a band of turbid water known as a “brown tide,” which damages reefs and seagrasses. At the same time, the foul odor and degraded beach appearance deter tourists, posing a significant challenge for one of the region’s main economic drivers. Public health is also affected: the algae can concentrate heavy metals such as arsenic, mercury, and cadmium, making it unsuitable for animal feed and posing contamination risks to aquifers if disposed of improperly.
Against this backdrop, the Caribe Circular initiative aims to revalorize up to 2Mt of sargassum by 2028, generating new value chains. Through industrialization, it is expected to create up to 3,500 direct jobs and integrate 80% of the state’s hotels into the use of sargassum-based products, consolidating a shared-responsibility model among the public, private, and social sectors.
IMIPAS’s next step will be to establish technical guidelines for proper sargassum management, including criteria for collection, processing, and utilization, with emphasis on sanitary standards, traceability, and regulatory compliance, key elements for integrating it into formal value chains. It will also generate data on potential uses, assessing its viability as an input across different industries, helping reduce technical uncertainty and guide investment under a sustainable framework.
The Caribe Circular initiative, considered one of the first multi-stakeholder alliances at the international level focused on sargassum industrialization, includes participation from the Mexican Caribbean Hotel Council, the National Chamber of the Restaurant and Seasoned Food Industry (Canirac), the Mexican Association of Women Entrepreneurs (Amexme) Cancun, and the Riviera Maya Hotel Association (AHRM).
At the regional level, these efforts are expected to generate economic opportunities for more than 20 affected countries, strengthening capacities, promoting technological innovation, and supporting regulatory frameworks adapted to each context, according to the IDB. The scientific protocols, predictive models, and regulatory approaches developed in the Mexican Caribbean provide a starting point for a management system that can be replicated across the wider Caribbean
articles.summary: Mexico is advancing a science-based, multi-stakeholder strategy to manage and industrialize sargassum through initiatives such as Caribe Circular, supported by research from IMIPAS and monitoring systems from UNAM. The effort seeks to integrate the macroalgae into regulated value chains while addressing environmental risks to coastal ecosystems and tourism, a key economic sector.

articles.title: Businesses Call On The EU To Deliver A Strong Circular Economy Act
articles.author: Forbes
articles.content:
Major businesses have called on the European Union (EU) to deliver a strong Circular Economy Act which will deliver ambitious regulatory proposals and create a true single market for circular solutions.
The EU Circular Economy Act aims to accelerate Europe’s transition to a circular economy, reduce dependencies on critical raw materials, and strengthen economic resilience.
Due for adoption later this year, the legislation also aims to double Europe’s circularity rate from its current figure of 12% to 24% by 2030.
A group of companies, in coordination with the Ellen MacArthur Foundation, recently delivered a joint letter to the European Commission, calling for ambitious regulatory proposals.
The letter states that circular business models are being held back by market fragmentation, inconsistent rules, and economic incentives that still favour linear approaches.
And it was signed by various businesses, including the LEGO Group, SAP and TOMRA.
The Ellen MacArthur Foundation also recently released a white paper setting out why the EU Circular Economy Act is a key opportunity for both European and national policymakers.
The Foundation’s business policy engagement lead, Carsten Wachholz, said the new EU legislation is important, because all the signs point to Europe missing its goal to double the share of secondary raw materials used to produce goods by 2030.
Wachholz added this trajectory comes at the same time as the EU wanting to become less dependent on imported materials, and growing concerns about supply chain disruptions due to wars and geopolitics.
“Companies are ready to invest, but they are hitting a wall, and these are always the same problems. Either markets are too small, or depend on whether you can transport used products, parts or secondary raw materials,” he told me.
Wachholz said the Circular Economy Act can change diverging definitions across different pieces of national waste legislation.
He added it can also provide additional guidance so that member states get to a common understanding about how these regulatory requirements should be implemented across the EU single market.
And he said it could also create a level playing field which puts circular business models on the same level as existing linear models, and allow companies to have more predictability and regulatory clarity to put the investments where they are needed, either in redesigning products, or in reverse logistics and recirculation.
“To bring it all together, businesses are asking for a market that works - consistent rules, fair pricing, and the kind of regulatory certainty that lets them invest at scale. These are the three big wins for the circular economy,” said Wachholz.
The chief executive and president of the recycling company TOMRA, Tove Andersen, said the upcoming EU Circular Economy Act is a vital opportunity to turn Europe’s circular ambitions into reality, in an email.
Andersen added the potential for Europe to be the global circularity leader through said commitment is evident.
“However, from our position at the centre of material recovery and circularity across plastics, metals and textiles, we see the same structural barriers repeatedly slowing the transition to a circular economy,” she added.
“To overcome these, the EU Circular Economy Act must create a true European single market for circular products and materials, aligning economic incentives such as VAT and procurement to favour circular choices.”
Angela Hultberg, global head of sustainability at Kearney said the EU Circular Economy Act will only be successful if it fixes the economics of circularity, in an email.
Hultberg added businesses need functioning markets for secondary materials, demand certainty, and regulation they can depend on for longer than four years.
“Without harmonised definitions, quality standards and consistent rules across borders, circularity will remain a project rather than a new way of handling goods,” she told me.
“Building the infrastructure needed will not be cheap, companies deserve to know there is a long-term plan in place. "
Hultberg added circularity means far more than recycling, which she said is where current policy seems to focus.
“The real gains come from all parts of the circularity spectrum, like durability, repair, reuse and remanufacturing,” she said.
“Mandatory recycling targets can help achieve scale quickly, and EU member states should lead by using public procurement to create demand.”
articles.summary: Major businesses have called on the European Union (EU) to deliver a strong Circular Economy Act which will deliver ambitious regulatory proposals and create a true single market for circular solutions. The EU Circular Economy Act aims to accelerate Europe’s transition to a circular economy, reduce dependencies on critical raw materials, and strengthen economic resilience.

articles.title: Divert Opens Washington Facility to Expand Circular Infrastructure for Unsold Food in Pacific Northwest
articles.author: The Packer
articles.content:
Divert Inc., a circular economy company on a mission to prevent food from being wasted, has opened its Integrated Diversion & Energy Facility in Longview, Wash., the first of its kind in the state. The 66,000 sq. ft. facility leverages Divert’s high-recovery depackaging technology and anaerobic digestion to process unsold food and organic materials into renewable energy and nutrient-rich fertilizers that support further food growth in the region. At full capacity, the facility will be capable of processing up to 100,000 tons of unsold, nondonatable food annually.
The facility expands clean energy and organics diversion infrastructure in the Pacific Northwest, creating a circular system that captures the value from uneaten food and keeps it in the regional economy. At capacity, the facility will transform the material it receives into over 235,000 MMBtu of renewable energy and 450,000 lb. of nutrient-rich fertilizer annually — enough to power over 3,200 homes and support the growth of 225 million lb. of apples. Divert’s facility helps bring Washington and Oregon closer to their goals to reduce wasted food and greenhouse gas emissions by offsetting up to 23,000 metric tons of CO2e each year through its operations. This advanced, purpose-built infrastructure will have impacts across the food value chain, from sending data upstream to facilitate source reduction and edible food recovery, to setting a new standard for downstream purity in land-applied soil amendments derived from food materials.
“The Longview facility will help build a more resilient, circular food system in the Pacific Northwest with energy, agriculture and economic impacts well beyond our operations,” says Ryan Begin, CEO and co-founder of Divert. “Across the country, waste systems are becoming more complex, and disposal is moving farther from where material is generated. We need solutions that keep value local. Our model is proven to increase food donation, recover energy and return nutrients back into the regional economy in an efficient, scalable way. That supports compliance, strengthens agricultural communities and advances greater energy independence.”
Through the new facility, Divert provides its integrated services to some of the largest food retailers and manufacturers in the Pacific Northwest, including Albertsons, Fred Meyer, Kroger, Reser’s Fine Foods, Safeway and more, while a partnership with Feeding America helps to optimize donation opportunities to people facing hunger in the local community.
“Our partnership with Divert and the new Longview facility give us an integrated organics diversion solution in the region we can rely on,” says Danelle Macias, senior director of sales and support for Albertsons, Portland Division. “Service reliability is essential to our business, and this is the kind of partnership where the operational details are taken care of, so we can focus on servicing our customers and communities.”
The facility also supports businesses navigating an expanding landscape of organics regulations, including Washington’s Organics Management Law and Portland’s business food scraps requirement, which require companies to divert organic waste from landfills.
“People often forget about the enormous climate impact of food production — and, by extension, food waste,” says Oregon metro councilor Christine Lewis. “By giving food scraps a circular-economy market option, Divert’s work elegantly addresses both halves of the equation. This is what innovation looks like.”
State leaders also emphasize the project’s impact on the regional workforce and long-term economic opportunity.
“For more than a decade, the Longview region has seen promising projects come and go, but Divert is different. It has followed through on its commitment to invest in this community,” says Heather Kurtenbach, executive secretary, Washington State Building and Construction Trades Council. “From the earliest stages, they partnered locally, prioritized our skilled workforce and ensured that good-paying construction jobs stayed right here in Longview. This project demonstrates that our region’s deep industrial roots and talented workforce can once again support major manufacturing investments and help lead Washington’s climate technology future.”
Longview, a major industrial region for the Pacific Northwest, offers close proximity to utilities capable of receiving renewable natural gas. Through an interconnection agreement with Cascade Natural Gas, RNG from the facility is fed directly into the existing distribution pipeline to power homes, businesses and hard-to-electrify industries in the area.
Divert is a portfolio company of Ara Partners, a global private equity, infrastructure and energy firm focused on decarbonizing the industrial economy. To learn more about Divert, click here.
articles.summary: Divert Inc., a circular economy company on a mission to prevent food from being wasted, has opened its Integrated Diversion & Energy Facility in Longview, Wash., the first of its kind in the state. The 66,000 sq. ft. facility leverages Divert’s high-recovery depackaging technology and anaerobic digestion to process unsold food and organic materials into renewable energy and nutrient-rich fertilizers that support further food growth in the region.

articles.title: Stellantis takes circular economy push to Morocco | Automotive World
articles.author: Automotive World
articles.content:
Stellantis has opened its first vehicle dismantling centre in the Middle East and Africa, a 6,000-square-metre facility in Casablanca, Morocco, with capacity to dismantle up to 10,000 vehicles per year. The €1.6m (US$1.8m) investment marks the OEM’s third dismantling site worldwide, after Turin, Italy, and São Paulo, Brazil, supporting around 150 direct and indirect jobs at full capacity.
The site sources end-of-life vehicles from insurance companies, auctions and other ELV channels, dismantling them into reusable parts (including traction batteries) for sale through Stellantis’ aftersales network and the B-Parts digital platform. The remaining material is collected for recycling.
The Casablanca centre forms part of Stellantis’ SUSTAINera circular economy business unit, which delivers remanufacturing, repairing, reuse and recycling services across the region. Stellantis said the site will serve Morocco and Sub-Saharan West Africa.
In a statement, Samir Cherfan, Chief Operating Officer Middle East & Africa and Global Head of Micromobility at Stellantis, said: “Circular Economy is a strategic priority for Stellantis in the Middle East and Africa. It enables us to combine industrial performance, affordability for customers and the responsible use of resources, while securing our long-term industrial footprint.”
The Casablanca facility is the first dismantling site of its kind launched by an OEM in Morocco, setting a benchmark for structured ELV management in the country.
Source: Stellantis

articles.title: Milken Institute and Motsepe Foundation Announce Winners of the $2 Million Milken-Motsepe Prize in AI and Manufacturing
articles.author: 01net
articles.content:
BleagLee, an AI-powered waste recycling company from Cameroon, receives $1 million Grand Prize for AI and manufacturing advancements; the Milken-Motsepe Prize also announces a new prize in circular economy
LOS ANGELES--(BUSINESS WIRE)--The Milken Institute and the Motsepe Foundation are honored to announce BleagLee, a Cameroon-based AI-powered waste recycling company, as the $1 million Grand Prize winner of the Milken-Motsepe Prize in AI and Manufacturing. The award is designed to recognize established companies driving innovation in Africa’s manufacturing sector with the potential to scale, create jobs, and spread the adoption of these technologies across the world. The winners were announced today at the Milken Institute Global Conference in Los Angeles.
BleagLee was awarded top honors for its work in leveraging AI-powered waste collection to convert plastic, agricultural, and e-waste into premium recycled products. Tanzania-based Freshpack Technologies was named the $250,000 Runner-Up for its AI-powered cold storage, which tackles food waste in Africa. Digitech Oasis Limited from the United Kingdom received $100,000 for the Most Advanced Use of 4IR, demonstrating technological capabilities that will shape competitive manufacturing over the next decade. Additional interim prizes totaling $750,000 were awarded and disbursed among five finalists, each receiving $30,000, and the 10 semifinalists, each receiving $50,000, throughout this prize cycle. All awards are unrestricted, enabling teams to direct their winnings toward what will most impact their businesses, strengthening their pipeline, speeding real-world pilots, and unlocking promising innovations.
BleagLee is revolutionizing waste management in Cameroon using patented AI software to detect and collect waste across communities and processing it into high-value products, such as engineered recycled polymers, 3D printing filaments, and bio-based carbon materials. By combining cutting-edge technology with community-driven impact, BleagLee is turning an environmental crisis into economic opportunity while working toward mitigating 300 million tons of CO2 equivalent emissions by 2030.
“Africa is producing world-class AI and technology innovation that is solving problems and creating opportunities on a global scale. And that story is only beginning to be told,” said Dr. Precious Moloi-Motsepe, co-founder and CEO, Motsepe Foundation. “When we invest in innovation that is both locally grounded and globally minded, the returns are limitless. I am delighted to see partnerships like this one ensure the brightest minds have the resources, networks, and platforms they need to scale their work and shape a more prosperous and equitable world.”
AI and Manufacturing is the fourth prize awarded as part of the Milken–Motsepe Innovation Prize Program, a series of competitive multimillion-dollar global competitions and awards designed to incentivize and reward bold, innovative technological solutions to address pressing economic and environmental challenges in Africa and across the globe.
Launched in May 2025, the Milken-Motsepe Prize in AI and Manufacturing attracted more than 2,000 entrepreneurs from 100 countries across five continents, with just 10 being selected as semifinalists.
Each team underwent a comprehensive judging process that evaluated four key criteria: commercial viability, operational economics, technological integration, and market scalability. In December 2025, 10 semifinalists pitched their innovations to investors at the Milken Institute Middle East and Africa Summit in Abu Dhabi. From this group, an expert panel of judges selected five finalists—BleagLee, Digitech Oasis Limited, Freshpack Technologies, Spiro, and Toto Safi Limited—to advance to the final stage of the innovation award, pitching their company’s innovations at the 2026 Milken Institute Global Conference.
Since its launch in 2021, the Milken-Motsepe Innovation Prize Program has awarded over $8 million in funding to more than 50 innovators worldwide. Participating teams have raised nearly 31 times the Grand Prize in additional outside investments, reaching and impacting over one million community members across the globe.
The Milken-Motsepe Innovation Prize Program offers free, curated resources and online events not only to award winners but also to more than 12,000 global entrepreneurs.
For more information about the winners and the Milken-Motsepe Innovation Prize Program, visit https://milkenmotsepeprize.org/.
Announcing a New Prize in Circular Economy
The next Milken-Motsepe Prize will focus on the circular economy, a new award designed to recognize companies using technology to enhance circular economy practices across a variety of industries. With $2 million in total prizes, including a $1 million Grand Prize, the Prize in Circular Economy seeks companies that develop and scale commercially viable, technology-enabled solutions that replace linear “take-make-waste” systems with regenerative, resource-efficient value chains.
The award also aims to address the complex realities of industrial waste management systems in Africa. Successful teams will demonstrate solutions that deliver measurable environmental and social impact, while providing training and reskilling opportunities to support safer, more specialized waste management practices.
“Our prize program has become a powerful engine for discovering and accelerating extraordinary innovators who are tackling some of the world’s most urgent challenges across industries,” said Emily Musil, PhD, managing director of Environmental and Social Innovation at the Milken Institute. “As we turn our focus to the Circular Economy, we are especially energized to champion entrepreneurs who are fundamentally reimagining how materials are used, recovered, and reused. These innovators are not only reducing waste—they are unlocking new economic value, strengthening local industries, and driving resilient, inclusive growth. As we enter our fifth year of the Milken-Motsepe Prize, we celebrate and acknowledge its growth—and its role in advancing solutions that deliver lasting benefits for communities, markets, and the environment.”
By extending the life cycle of materials, strengthening local manufacturing, and improving both upstream and downstream waste management systems, the prize seeks to accelerate the transition to a more sustainable and inclusive circular economy in Africa.
Registration is open now through August 13, 2026, 2 p.m. Eastern. To apply, visit: https://milkenmotsepeprize.org/circular-economy/.
The Milken-Motsepe Innovation Prize Program seeks companies that must meet the following eligibility requirements: have over two years of continuous operation, generate over $500,000 in revenue and raised capital, have institutional, corporate, and/or public‑sector partnerships, has a solution currently deployed on the African continent, has clear evidence of social impact and job creation, and demonstrates operational readiness to deploy more than $1 million in funding.
Teams from a variety of businesses are encouraged to apply, and teams will be required to submit vertical-specific metrics from industries such as food systems, packaging, electronics, fashion and textiles, construction, and the built environment.
About the Milken Institute
The Milken Institute is a nonprofit, nonpartisan think tank focused on accelerating measurable progress on the path to a meaningful life. With a focus on financial, physical, mental, and environmental health, we bring together the best ideas and innovative resourcing to develop blueprints for tackling some of our most critical global issues through the lens of what’s pressing now and what’s coming next. For more information, visit https://milkeninstitute.org.
About the Motsepe Foundation
The Motsepe Foundation was founded in 1999 by Dr. Patrice Motsepe and his wife, Dr. Precious Moloi-Motsepe. The goal of the Motsepe Foundation is to contribute toward eradicating poverty and to sustainably improve the living conditions and standards of living of poor, unemployed, and marginalized people in South Africa, Africa, and the world. In January 2013, Dr. Motsepe and Dr. Moloi-Motsepe joined the Giving Pledge, which was started by Warren Buffett and Bill and Melinda Gates. Dr. Motsepe and his wife committed to give half of their wealth to the poor and for philanthropic purposes during their lifetime and beyond. For more information, visit https://www.motsepefoundation.org/.
Contacts

Limiller@milkeninstitute.org

articles.title: Europe Travel Industry Faces Sustainability Shock As Major Global Companies Push European Union Toward Radical Circular Economy Transformation To Protect Tourism Supply Chains And Reduce Waste: New Updates - Travel And Tour World
articles.author: Travel And Tour World
articles.content:
The European travel and tourism industry is moving toward a dramatic transformation as some of the world’s largest corporations intensify pressure on the European Union to introduce an ambitious new Circular Economy Act capable of reshaping how businesses operate across the continent. The proposed legislation is rapidly becoming one of the most important economic and environmental developments affecting tourism, hospitality, aviation, transport, and destination infrastructure across Europe.
Major international corporations including The LEGO Group, SAP, and TOMRA have publicly backed the initiative through coordinated action led by the Ellen MacArthur Foundation. Their collective warning is clear. Europe risks falling behind in sustainability, resource security, and long-term tourism resilience unless urgent regulatory reforms are introduced to support a fully functioning circular economy.
The proposed law seeks to dramatically increase Europe’s use of recycled and reused materials while reducing dependence on imported raw resources. Officials and industry leaders increasingly believe the shift could become a defining moment for the future of European travel and tourism infrastructure.
According to policy goals outlined by the European Commission, Europe aims to double its circular material usage rate from approximately 12 percent to 24 percent before the end of the decade. Government-backed sustainability frameworks published by the European Union have identified circularity as a strategic priority for economic stability, industrial competitiveness, and climate resilience.
Advertisement
The travel and tourism industry stands directly in the path of this economic revolution. Hotels, airlines, cruise operators, rail companies, airports, restaurants, and tourism infrastructure developers all depend heavily on global supply chains vulnerable to rising costs, geopolitical disruptions, and raw material shortages.
A stronger circular economy could significantly reduce operational risks for Europe’s tourism sector by encouraging reuse, refurbishment, recycling, and localized production systems. Hospitality operators are increasingly facing pressure to reduce waste, eliminate single-use products, and improve sustainability credentials as travelers become more environmentally conscious.
Advertisement
Advertisement
European tourism destinations are also under mounting pressure to balance visitor growth with environmental protection. Governments across Europe have accelerated sustainability targets for transport systems, urban infrastructure, and tourism facilities. The proposed Circular Economy Act is expected to play a major role in supporting those objectives.
The European Union has already emphasized through official sustainability frameworks that circularity can reduce greenhouse gas emissions, strengthen domestic manufacturing capacity, and improve resource efficiency across major industries linked to travel and tourism.
Despite growing enthusiasm around sustainable business models, major corporations argue that Europe’s current system still rewards waste-heavy production and outdated linear consumption patterns. Companies involved in the initiative say investment opportunities are being blocked by fragmented regulations and inconsistent standards across EU member states.
Executives supporting the Circular Economy Act argue that businesses attempting to scale sustainable operations continue to face expensive administrative barriers when transporting used materials, recycled goods, and repairable products across European borders. Many industry leaders believe these obstacles are slowing innovation and discouraging investment.
For the tourism industry, these barriers create additional challenges. Hotel chains attempting to source recycled furnishings, airlines pursuing sustainable cabin upgrades, and transport operators investing in reusable infrastructure often encounter complicated compliance systems that vary from one country to another.
The business coalition wants the European Union to establish what it describes as a true single market for circular solutions, allowing sustainable materials and products to move more freely across Europe. Supporters argue this would help tourism-related businesses cut costs while improving sustainability performance.
Advertisement
Advertisement
The push for circular reform comes at a time of growing concern about global supply chain instability. International conflicts, shipping disruptions, rising energy prices, and geopolitical tensions have exposed vulnerabilities throughout Europe’s industrial and tourism networks.
Tourism businesses remain particularly sensitive to supply chain shocks because the sector relies heavily on imported materials, construction products, transport equipment, food systems, and energy-intensive operations. The hospitality industry has already experienced significant cost pressures linked to inflation and logistical disruption.
Supporters of the Circular Economy Act believe Europe can protect its tourism economy by increasing domestic reuse of materials instead of depending heavily on external imports. Recycled metals, refurbished equipment, recovered plastics, and circular manufacturing systems could help stabilize costs while improving environmental performance.
The European Commission has repeatedly highlighted the importance of strategic autonomy and resource efficiency in its official sustainability agenda. Government policy documents emphasize that circularity can help Europe reduce exposure to international market volatility while supporting economic resilience.
The timing of the proposed legislation is critical because traveler expectations are rapidly evolving. Across Europe, tourism boards, destination authorities, and hospitality operators are under pressure to demonstrate meaningful environmental action.
Modern travelers increasingly favor destinations and businesses that promote sustainable practices, reduced waste, energy efficiency, and environmentally responsible tourism experiences. This shift is pushing tourism-dependent economies to modernize infrastructure faster than ever before.
Advertisement
Advertisement
Cities investing in sustainable mobility systems, eco-friendly accommodation, recycling programs, and green transport networks could gain significant competitive advantages in the global tourism market. Industry analysts believe destinations that fail to adapt may struggle to attract environmentally conscious travelers in the coming years.
The Circular Economy Act could accelerate investment in greener tourism infrastructure by creating stronger financial incentives for reuse, repair, recycling, and sustainable manufacturing across Europe’s travel economy.
Although momentum behind the legislation is growing, experts warn that Europe remains at risk of missing its long-term circularity goals if policymakers fail to introduce ambitious reforms quickly enough.
Industry leaders supporting the initiative argue that incremental policy adjustments will not be sufficient to transform Europe’s economic structure. They believe sweeping regulatory modernization is required to unlock large-scale investment and remove outdated barriers preventing sustainable growth.
The proposed legislation is expected to move through critical stages later this year, with policymakers facing intense pressure from environmental groups, corporate leaders, manufacturing sectors, and tourism stakeholders alike.
For Europe’s travel and tourism industry, the outcome could define the next decade of sustainability policy, infrastructure investment, and supply chain security. A successful Circular Economy Act could help create a more resilient tourism economy capable of withstanding future disruptions while supporting Europe’s environmental ambitions.
Advertisement
Advertisement
At the same time, failure to act decisively could leave the region increasingly vulnerable to rising operational costs, resource shortages, and global supply chain instability that threaten the long-term future of European tourism competitiveness.
As pressure intensifies in Brussels, the battle over Europe’s circular economy future is no longer just about recycling policy. It is rapidly becoming a defining economic struggle over how the continent will power, protect, and sustain its travel and tourism industry in an era of growing global uncertainty.

articles.title: Energy Independence Begins with Education
articles.author: The Baltic Times
articles.content:
Fuel price fluctuations over recent months have become a constant reality. The conflict in the Middle East, affecting the Strait of Hormuz - one of the world’s most important oil transit routes - is also being felt in the everyday lives of people in Latvia. While fuel price increases across the European Union have varied in intensity, the rise in Latvia has been particularly notable. For example, at the end of April, Latvia had the 11th highest average diesel price in the EU (€2.006 per litre), significantly exceeding even neighbouring Estonia (€1.878 per litre). Rising fuel prices have heavily affected other sectors as well, including transport companies, whose monthly expenses have increased by approximately €700,000. Given that markets continue to react to every development related to the conflict, and a calm, stable geopolitical environment currently feels almost utopian, it is necessary to look for long-term solutions - and one of them is the circular economy.
Is Climate Neutrality Possible?
It is no secret that the European Union has set ambitious targets in renewable and alternative energy in order to achieve climate neutrality by 2050. However, the EU currently produces only 43% of its energy, while more than half (57%) is imported, much of it consisting of fossil resources: oil and petroleum products (38%) and natural gas (21%). This means that every geopolitical disruption is immediately reflected in prices, making the transition to alternative energy not only a logical and environmentally responsible step, but at times seemingly the only viable solution. Nevertheless, there are still sceptics who argue that climate neutrality is unattainable.
Every Solution Has Its Shadow Side
From a theoretical perspective, climate neutrality is achievable because we already possess the four key prerequisites - sunlight, wind, technological capabilities, and scientific advancement. In practice, however, achieving this goal will only be possible if it is accompanied by efforts to address economic growth and competitiveness challenges, while simultaneously investing in relevant education and academic programmes.
Climate neutrality and alternative energy represent the end goal, but every solution also has its shadow side. Lithium and other battery materials such as cobalt and nickel are extracted with considerable impact on ecosystems and intensive water consumption. Likewise, the production of wind turbines generates relatively high emissions, while their transportation and installation still largely rely on fossil fuels.
In the “Circular Economy and Social Entrepreneurship” programme, we discuss these aspects with students in order to strengthen their competencies and encourage critical evaluation of sustainability solutions throughout their entire life cycle, not only by looking at the final result. This means developing the ability to make informed, data-driven decisions while balancing environmental, economic, and social considerations, as well as understanding the compromises that inevitably accompany the green transition. It is precisely this approach that allows us to prepare specialists capable not only of implementing innovative solutions, but also of responsibly assessing their long-term impact.
A Place Where Sustainability Solutions Are Put into Practice
The alternative energy sector, as well as the circular economy more broadly, is still a relatively new and rapidly developing field. For education to keep pace with these developments, close cooperation with industry professionals, opinion leaders, and experts working on real-world projects is essential.
Students from various countries studying in the programme often point out that Latvia is highly advanced in this area. Compared to many other countries, Latvia already has a relatively high share of renewable energy, practical examples of circular economy solutions are available, and the social entrepreneurship ecosystem is also actively developing. Latvia is a place where sustainability solutions are implemented in practice rather than remaining merely topics for discussion. This, in turn, creates additional motivation to continue developing the sector by strengthening cooperation between education, business, and the public sector.
Fuel price volatility clearly demonstrates how vulnerable an economy based on imported fossil resources can be. Every geopolitical disruption immediately translates into real costs for both businesses and residents, and this instability is likely to persist in the future. Therefore, the transition to alternative energy and the implementation of circular economy principles are not merely environmental issues - they are also matters of economic security and competitiveness. The faster we develop local, sustainable solutions and educate specialists capable of implementing them in practice, the less dependent we will become on global crises and price fluctuations in the future.
articles.summary: Fuel price fluctuations over recent months have become a constant reality. The conflict in the Middle East, affecting the Strait of Hormuz - one of the world’s most important oil transit routes - is also being felt in the everyday lives of people in Latvia. While fuel price increases across the European Union have varied in intensity, the rise in Latvia has been particularly notable.

articles.title: Energy Transition and Circular Economy: A Path to Decarbonization
articles.author: Mexico Business News
articles.content:
STORY INLINE POST
In a world of constant change and evolving concepts, two new key players have emerged: the energy transition and the circular economy. At first glance, they may appear unrelated; however, they go hand in hand, sharing common interests and leading to regulatory convergence. The circular economy reduces the need to manufacture new parts, which in turn reduces industrial energy consumption, thereby helping the energy transition to achieve its decarbonization targets more quickly.
To gain a better understanding, we can start by recognizing that the energy transition is a process of structural change in energy production and consumption systems, aimed at moving from an energy mix based on fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) to one with low or zero carbon emissions, supported by renewable sources, while the circular economy is a model of production and consumption that seeks to extend the useful life of products and eliminate waste, unlike a traditional linear model (extract-manufacture-dispose), the circular economy is based on the principles of reduce, reuse, repair, and recycle.
Both the energy transition and the circular economy have benefits and challenges that can affect their implementation and development. Let’s start with the benefits. The energy transition: a) Climate change mitigation, based on a drastic reduction in carbon dioxide and greenhouse gas emissions, b) Energy security, based on reducing dependence on fossil fuel imports by harnessing local resources such as the sun and water, and c) Technology, based on driving the development of batteries, green hydrogen and smart grids. On the other hand, the limitations or opposing factors include: a) Intermittency of renewable sources; solar and wind sources do not always generate energy, which requires costly storage systems, b) Initial cost, which is high as it requires massive investment in infrastructure and the modernisation of electricity grids, and c) Mining impact, with the need to manufacture solar panels and turbines that require large quantities of minerals (lithium, cobalt and rare earths).
As for the benefits of the circular economy: a) Resource efficiency, which aims to reduce dependence on virgin raw materials, b) Cost savings, as companies reduce costs by recovering materials and optimizing processes, resulting in a new business model that promotes rental services rather than purchasing, as well as fostering and boosting the repair and reuse industry. What are the downsides of the circular economy? a) Logistical complexity, as it is necessary to design systems for the return and recovery of materials, which can be complex and costly, b) Design barriers, as many products are designed with planned obsolescence in mind, making them difficult to recycle; and finally, c) Culture, as a shift in consumer perception is required to change their consumption and ownership habits.
Driven by technical regulations, both the energy transition and the circular economy are forcing a reworking of standards to ensure that technology is not only functional but also environmentally friendly and operationally stable, leading to an impact on regulations such as grid codes, energy storage and distributed generation for the energy transition, and on ecodesign, special waste management and certification of recycled materials for the circular economy, whilst job skills are also evolving due to the need to develop new profiles for hybrid system installers, circularity auditors and specialized preventive maintenance technicians, in addition to requiring constant updating of the administrative regulatory framework, which is in a state of constant flux, technical standards are becoming the cornerstone of reliability for training and assessment centers, ensuring that processes follow best practice; Humanity is currently undergoing an evolutionary process in which the challenge is great, yet the need and the new social era demand it: a world with ecosystems that mutually support one another’s stability without undermining each other’s existence.
articles.summary: STORY INLINE POST In a world of constant change and evolving concepts, two new key players have emerged: the energy transition and the circular economy. At first glance, they may appear unrelated; however, they go hand in hand, sharing common interests and leading to regulatory convergence. The circular economy reduces the need to manufacture new parts, which in turn reduces industrial energy consumption, thereby helping the energy transition to achieve its decarbonization targets more quickly.

articles.title: EU envoy urges circular economy shift to cut costs for firms and fosters innovation
articles.author: daily-sun.com
articles.content:
EU envoy urges circular economy shift to cut costs for firms and fosters innovation
Daily Sun Report, Dhaka
Published: 06 May 2026, 01:48 PM
European Union (EU) Ambassador to Bangladesh Michael Miller. Photo: Kamrul Islam Ratan
European Union (EU) Ambassador to Bangladesh Michael Miller on Wednesday said adopting circular economy practices including recycling, material substitution and enhanced resource productivity can reduce costs for firms and fosters innovation.
He made the remarks at seminar on accelerating circular transition trough Switch2ce pilot pathways in Bangladesh organised by ministry of Commerce and BGMEA in cooperation with H&M group, Best Seller supported by UNIDO at Intercontinental hotel in Dhaka.
Miller said resource efficiency is both an economic strategy and an environmental necessity, noting that the EU, like Bangladesh, relies heavily on imported raw materials and energy.
He warned that global trade is becoming increasingly uncertain and stressed the need to diversify supply chains.
Highlighting the EU’s goal of achieving carbon neutrality by 2050, he said circularity is central to its growth strategy, aiming to decouple economic expansion from resource use.
Referring to the textile sector, Miller noted that the EU generates over 5 million tonnes of textile waste annually, while Bangladesh produces around 600,000 tonnes. He said EU policies on sustainable textiles would have implications for Bangladesh, its largest export market.
He reaffirmed the EU’s commitment to supporting Bangladesh’s transition through investment, policy support and skills development initiatives.

articles.title: LIFE: driving innovation, autonomy and resilience for a competitive Europe
articles.author: European Climate, Infrastructure and Environment Executive Agency
articles.content:
The latest LIFE publication, LIFE and the EU’s Competitiveness Agenda: Fostering innovation, strategic autonomy, and resilience for sustainable growth, showcases projects from across Europe that demonstrate how environmental and climate action can drive economic value. From circular economy solutions in Finland to zero-emission mobility in Italy, these projects illustrate how LIFE helps bring innovations to market and scale them up.
By bridging the gap between research and deployment, LIFE enables the uptake of clean technologies, strengthens value chains and supports the creation of new market opportunities – helping to turn sustainability into a competitive advantage for Europe.
Supporting the EU Competitiveness Compass
With a budget of €5.4 billion for 2021-2027 and over €4 billion mobilised since 2014, the LIFE Programme acts as a catalyst for investment and deployment, mobilising both public and private financing. It supports the objectives of the EU’s Competitiveness Compass by helping close the gap between innovation and market uptake, accelerating decarbonisation and reducing strategic dependencies.
Innovation, strategic autonomy and enhanced resilience
LIFE drives innovation by supporting the deployment and scale-up of market-ready solutions, especially regarding circular economy, clean technologies and sustainable business models.
For example, DeliverEEM is scaling up energy-efficient mortgage markets across Europe and mobilising private investment for building renovation, while PlastLIFE is advancing circular plastics solutions and reducing dependence on fossil-based materials.
LIFE also strengthens strategic autonomy by reducing reliance on imported energy and raw materials, while supporting European industrial capacity and circular value chains. This is seen through projects such as EXQUISHEAT, which promotes industrial heat pump solutions to reduce fossil fuel dependence, and LIFE-SYNFLUOR, which transforms industrial waste into critical raw materials, helping secure EU supply chains.
LIFE enhances resilience by supporting climate adaptation, resource security and sustainable ecosystems, which underpin long-term economic stability. For example, LIFE TreeCheck strengthens urban climate resilience through green infrastructure, while LIFE Olivares Vivos + demonstrates how biodiversity can improve agricultural productivity and competitiveness.
Together, these projects show how LIFE turns environmental ambition into economic opportunity - supporting innovation, strengthening Europe’s autonomy by reducing dependencies and building resilience, including through more efficient use of resources and circular solutions across key sectors of the economy.

From circular economy solutions in Finland to zero-emission mobility in Italy, these projects illustrate how LIFE helps bring innovations to market and scale them up.

articles.title: Tetra Pak, SIMEPRODE Partner on Recycling in Nuevo Leon
articles.author: Mexico Business News
articles.content:
Tetra Pak and the Integral System for the Ecological Management and Processing of Resources (SIMEPRODE) formalized a strategic agreement to strengthen the recovery and recycling of food and beverage carton packaging in Nuevo Leon, aiming to integrate these materials back into industrial value chains under a circular economy model.
The agreement focuses on optimizing the collection, separation and processing of Tetra Pak cartons to prevent landfill disposal and enable their reuse as secondary raw materials. The collaboration aligns with Tetra Pak’s global sustainability strategy to develop more efficient and scalable systems for collection, recycling and material valorization.
The initiative includes coordinated actions to improve waste separation at the source and expand recovery through SIMEPRODE’s sorting plant and collection points under the Rutas Verdes (Green Routes) program. It also provides for infrastructure upgrades, technical training, knowledge-sharing and environmental education campaigns to increase public participation in recycling.
A central component of the partnership is the consolidation of recycling value chains through collaboration with specialized companies, expanding the transformation of used cartons into products such as paper, cardboard tubes, roofing sheets, permeable flooring, alternative wood, urban furniture and industrial inputs.
Both parties will also assess the adoption of new technologies to enhance collection, sorting and recycling processes, drawing on international models. Monitoring and evaluation mechanisms will be implemented to track progress, identify improvements and scale solutions.
“For Tetra Pak, the circular economy is not an aspirational concept, but an operational priority that requires solutions at scale and collaboration among key stakeholders. This alliance with SIMEPRODE reflects our commitment to promoting more robust recycling systems, where each recovered package is reintegrated into new value chains, generating measurable environmental and economic impact,” said Guillermo Pugliese, Director of Sustainability for Tetra Pak Mexico, Andean and Central America & Caribbean.
Francisco Silva, Director General, SIMEPRODE, said the agreement advances a more efficient and inclusive circular economy model. “Collaboration between government and the private sector is key to strengthening our capabilities in comprehensive waste management, particularly in recycling and recovery, to reduce the amount of waste sent to landfills. With this agreement, we continue to add partners and move toward a more efficient, sustainable and inclusive model for the benefit of society and a circular economy model for the state of Nuevo Leon,” he said.
Under the agreement, Tetra Pak will ensure that recovered packaging is reintroduced into production cycles, maximizing material value and supporting the transition toward more sustainable production and consumption models in Nuevo Leon
articles.summary: Tetra Pak and the Integral System for the Ecological Management and Processing of Resources (SIMEPRODE) formalized a strategic agreement to strengthen the recovery and recycling of food and beverage carton packaging in Nuevo Leon, aiming to integrate these materials back into industrial value chains under a circular economy model.

articles.title: Hoping to Do Their Part in the Circular Economy: A
articles.author: gehealthcare.com
articles.content:
Don't have an account?
At a GE HealthCare manufacturing plant in Ciudad Juárez, Mexico, machines churn out blood-pressure cuffs at the dizzying rate of 1.4 million per week. One of the final steps in the process is trimming the edge of the cuff so it looks good and feels comfortable for the patient.
As production has ramped up, so have the piles of trimmings — reaching 624 tons of material a year. The trimmings are currently made of new PVC plastic. And international law requires them to be returned from Mexico to the United States, where at present they are buried in a landfill, costing the facility $52,000 annually.
But managers atthe plant have found a more sustainable solution. Instead of dumping the leftover PVC, they are working with companies in Mexico to transform it into a new product: the soles of shoes. They want their initiative to be a model for reducing waste, saving money, and helping GE HealthCare achieve its environmental, social, and governance (ESG) goals.
Ramiro Alcoverde is the environmental, health, and safety (EHS) manager for GE HealthCare’s Border Operations facilities, which encompass the plant in Ciudad Juárez and two other sites, one in Mexico and one in the U.S. He coordinates the return of leftover materials for 79 different products, making sure the plants comply with the customs, legal, and financial regulations of both countries.
Alcoverde had been exploring ways to recycle or reuse by-products for a long time. Years ago, he had looked into using leftover Thermadrape, a type of warming blanket, to help children in Central American hospitals, but the rules regarding medical products were too stringent and he couldn’t get the project approved.
A different perspective helped him find a way forward. In 2021, Alcoverde and Enrique Pineda, a Border Ops plant manager based in El Paso, Texas, were approached by a company called Recilogic in Chihuahua, Mexico. The business specializes in finding profitable uses for industrial by-products.
“We know for a fact that you are disposing of clean PVC from your blood-pressure cuffs,” Alcoverde recalls the representative saying, “and we think that the shoe industry in Mexico could take advantage of your by-product.”
Alcoverde and Pineda agreed to test several pounds of the PVC with a manufacturer in Guanajuato, in central Mexico. Through experiments, the company found that a mixture consisting of 60% of the trimmings from the blood-pressure cuffs, combined with special resins and adhesives, formed a strong and flexible shoe sole.
“The beauty around this project is that typically the recycling industry is not, I would say, very clean,” Alcoverde explains. “They receive a lot of mixed plastics and need to wash and clean them. Because we are a medical-grade industry producing medical-grade scraps, our by-product is very clean, and they are really happy for that.”
The first shoes using the leftover PVC were produced in November. Today, workers at the Ciudad Juárez plant gather the trimmings in large drums for Recilogic, which shreds the material and sends it along to the shoe-sole maker.
“When people come to visit the site and we tell them that we are doing this, you can notice the pride and emotion in whoever is sharing the story, from the plant manager to the business team leader,” Alcoverde says. “We are making this world cleaner.”
While the project is promising, he continues to navigate challenges. The business is used to selling finished goods, not by-products, so GE HealthCare’s customs and financial teams have had to work out how to invoice for the PVC material and how to conform with customs regulations to sell directly to other companies in Mexico, rather than importing raw materials into Mexico and exporting finished goods to the United States.
Alcoverde and Pineda want to apply what they have learned to creating reuses for other by-products. They have another type of leftover plastic that they think might be suitable for construction. They also are contributing to the efforts of Chihuahua Green City, a Mexican nongovernmental organization that promotes recycling and finding new applications for excess materials. The larger goal is to create a circular economy, in which waste is minimized, and recycling or downcycling is built into the manufacturing process. Supported by the European Union in Mexico, Chihuahua Green City helps businesses comply with the Paris Agreement on climate change, which aims to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels.
Alcoverde encourages managers at other plants to contribute to these types of efforts. “As the circular economy brings a new mindset, it’s a new value for GE HealthCare,” he says. “It’s not only about being cost-efficient with the core business at your site, but there might be several entrepreneurial opportunities using the by-products, or there might be opportunities for greening the supply chain.”

One of the final steps in the process is trimming the edge of the cuff so it looks good and feels comfortable for the patient. As production has ramped up, so have the piles of trimmings — reaching 624 tons of material a year. The trimmings are currently made of new PVC plastic.

articles.title: Over 50 businesses urge government to publish Circular Economy Growth Plan
articles.author: Circular Online
articles.content:
Over 50 businesses and trade associations, including IKEA and Virgin Media O2, are urging the UK Government to publish the long-delayed Circular Economy Growth Plan.
As part of the joint letter, the businesses said the plan would end uncertainty, provide ‘the confidence to invest’ and accelerate a circular economy transition across their operations.
The Circular Economy Growth Plan was originally expected to be published in October last year and has been held back for over six months.
Circular Online learned that the Department for the Environment, Food, and Rural Affairs (Defra) expected to publish the plan for consultation in early 2026. However, it has yet to be published, and there is no indication of when it could arrive.
The businesses have said they are worried the ongoing delay ‘will harm momentum towards a more resilient, resource efficient economy’.
The plan has been developed by the Circular Economy Taskforce, an independent advisory group comprising experts and leaders from various sectors.
The letter has been signed by businesses including IKEA and Virgin Media O2, as well as the Chartered Institution of Wastes Management (CIWM).
Rachel Solomon Williams, Executive Director at Aldersgate Group, a signatory of the letter, commented: “The continued delay to the Circular Economy Growth Plan is creating real uncertainty for business.”
“We need a clear, cross‑government, long‑term approach that provides policy certainty, supports resilience, and enables investment.”
“This is particularly important as the UK seeks to reset its relationship with the EU: policy divergence can cause substantial practical and economic challenges for business.”
The joint letter was sent to Emma Reynolds, Secretary of State for Defra, as well as the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, Department for Transport, Treasury, and Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government.
Last week, a separate letter coordinated by The Restart Project and signed by Green Alliance, Back Market, and the CIWM also called on the Prime Minister to release the Circular Economy Growth Plan.
articles.summary: Over 50 businesses and trade associations, including IKEA and Virgin Media O2, are urging the UK Government to publish the long-delayed Circular Economy Growth Plan. As part of the joint letter, the businesses said the plan would end uncertainty, provide ‘the confidence to invest’ and accelerate a circular economy transition across their operations. The Circular Economy Growth Plan was originally expected to be published in October last year and has been held back for over six months.

articles.title: European Businesses Call for "Teeth" in New Circular Economy Act
articles.author: streamlinefeed.co.ke
articles.content:
We're loading the full news article for you. This includes the article content, images, author information, and related articles.
Over 150 European companies demand a stronger Circular Economy Act with mandatory "Right to Repair" laws. The move could reshape global trade and supply chains.
A powerful coalition of over 150 European businesses, including retail giants and tech innovators, has issued an urgent call to the European Union to deliver a "strong and enforceable" Circular Economy Act. The group argues that without mandatory standards for product durability and "Right to Repair," the continent will fail its climate targets and remain dangerously dependent on volatile global raw material markets.
The proposed Act aims to decouple economic growth from resource consumption—a radical shift from the traditional "take-make-dispose" model. By mandating that all products sold in the EU be easily repairable, recyclable, and made from non-toxic materials, the legislation would fundamentally reshape global supply chains, affecting every manufacturer from Shenzhen to Stuttgart.
The push for a stronger Act is not just an environmental crusade; it is a calculated economic strategy. Business leaders argue that a circular economy could unlock €600 billion (approx. KES 85 trillion) in annual savings for EU businesses and create over 700,000 new jobs by 2030. In a world where the prices of rare earth minerals and lithium are subject to geopolitical whims, the ability to "mine" old products for materials is a matter of national security.
However, the business coalition warns that voluntary measures have failed. They are demanding a "level playing field" where companies that invest in sustainable design are not undercut by cheap, disposable imports. Their demands include a mandatory "Digital Product Passport" that tracks a product’s material composition and environmental footprint throughout its entire lifecycle.
The implications for Kenya and the wider East African region are profound. The EU is one of Kenya’s largest trading partners, and any new standards on product design will immediately become "de facto" requirements for Kenyan exporters. More importantly, the EU’s "Right to Repair" movement aligns with Kenya’s own vibrant "Jua Kali" sector, which has specialized in repair and upcycling for decades.
If the EU succeeds in standardizing repairable electronics, it could significantly reduce the flow of illegal e-waste that often ends up in African landfills. Instead of receiving "obsolete" tech, Kenya could benefit from a global market of high-quality, modular devices that are easier to maintain locally. This creates a "Green Bridge" where sustainable design in the North supports the circular economies of the South.
Despite the business support, the Circular Economy Act faces stiff opposition from sectors built on fast-consumption models. Lobbyists for some consumer electronics and "fast fashion" brands argue that the mandates will stifle innovation and increase prices for low-income consumers. The European Commission must now navigate these competing interests while maintaining the Act’s "teeth."
As the final draft of the Act approaches a vote in the European Parliament, the world is watching. If the EU can prove that a "circular" GDP is not only possible but more profitable, it will provide the blueprint for the next century of global trade. For businesses, the message is clear: the age of the disposable is over.

articles.title: Over 50 firms push UK Government to publish delayed circular economy plan - edie
articles.author: edie.net
articles.content:
In the letter, sent to the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) Secretary of State Emma Reynolds today (6 May), over 50 leading businesses and trade associations have urged the UK Government to publish the long-awaited Circular Economy Growth Plan “as soon as possible”.
Signatories include leaders from the British Plastics Federation (BPF), IKEA, Michelin, SUEZ, Veolia, Tech UK, the UK Fashion and Textile Association and the UK Green Building Council (UKGBC).
The authors express concern that the “ongoing delay” to the plan’s publication “could harm momentum towards a more resilient, resource-efficient economy”, calling for a “clear and ambitious signal from the government” to accelerate the circular transition across businesses.
“At a time when we need every tool in the box to create greater economic resilience, holding back on this transformative plan makes no sense. It’s an obvious way to protect business supply chains, stimulate jobs and growth and keep prices down for consumers,” explained Libby Peake, the head of resources and senior fellow at think tank Green Alliance.
More delays, more uncertainty
The Plan, previously called the Circular Economy Strategy, was first announced in March 2025, with the goal of giving “businesses the certainty to plan and the confidence to build and invest in new infrastructure”. It aims to build on the work of the Circular Economy Taskforce, launched in late 2024.
Initially planned for publication in October that year, in September 2025, following the cabinet reshuffle, the Government pushed the date back further to early 2026.
“From our work with manufacturers, SMEs and fashion and textiles brands, we are seeing how uncertainty is holding back investment and making it harder to scale circular solutions, co-founder of WEFT and signatory of the letter, Kristina Bull said. “Our recent consumer research shows that policy design can influence behaviour, but that affordability and practicality remain central to how people make purchasing decisions. Government now needs to match industry intent with a plan that is not only published quickly, but ambitious enough to give businesses the confidence to invest and move forward.”
As Trevor Hutchings, the CEO of Renewable Energy and Clean Technology (REA), explained, boosting circularity is also critical to bolster the UK’s supply chain resilience.“The war in the Middle East highlights the need to reduce our reliance on concentrated international supply chains and to make better use of our own resources by moving to a circular economy. By increasing the circular management of critical minerals, biodegradable wastes and other resources, we can turn a domestic challenge into a strategic asset.
Without clear direction on circular economy targets and suggested approaches, there are concerns that the UK (and England in particular) will fall behind the progress of surrounding nations.
“We need a clear, cross‑government, long‑term approach that provides policy certainty, supports resilience, and enables investment,” said Rachel Solomon Williams, director of the Aldersgate Group. “This is particularly important as the UK seeks to reset its relationship with the EU: policy divergence can cause substantial practical and economic challenges for business.”

Signatories include leaders from the British Plastics Federation (BPF), IKEA, Michelin, SUEZ, Veolia, Tech UK, the UK Fashion and Textile Association and the UK Green Building Council (UKGBC).

articles.content:
PCR-Based Circular Supply Chain Platforms Enter an Enterprise Integration Phase: Why Digital Traceability, Compliance Mandates, and Data Infrastructure Are Reshaping a $4.3 Billion Market
Get detailed market forecasts, competitive benchmarking, and pricing trends:

Quick Stats Snapshot
• Market Size (2026): USD 1.2 billion
• Forecast (2036): USD 4.3 billion
• CAGR (2026-2036): 13.7%
• Incremental Opportunity: USD 3.1 billion
• Leading End Use: End-to-end PCR sourcing (45% share)
• Top Platform Model: Circular supply chain platforms (50% share)
• Fastest Growing Regions: India (15.4%), China (14.6%)
Market Size and Forecast: High Growth Driven by Compliance Digitization
The PCR-based circular supply chain platform market is projected to expand from USD 1.2 billion in 2026 to USD 4.3 billion by 2036, reflecting a CAGR of 13.7%. This accelerated growth is not cyclical it is structural. Regulatory frameworks such as digital product passports and extended producer responsibility requirements are making traceability and verification systems mandatory for market access.
As a result, organizations are shifting from fragmented, manual tracking methods to integrated digital platforms capable of managing complex, multi-tier supply chains. These platforms are evolving into core enterprise systems, linking procurement, compliance, sustainability reporting, and operational decision-making.
Key Growth Drivers: Regulation, Risk, and Data Transparency
1. Regulatory Mandates for Traceability and Compliance
Governments are increasingly requiring auditable proof of recycled content and material flows. Digital product passport frameworks and sustainability reporting standards are transforming traceability into a legal requirement rather than a voluntary practice.
2. Corporate Risk Management and ESG Accountability
Companies face growing exposure to regulatory penalties and reputational risks linked to unverifiable sustainability claims. Platforms provide secure, auditable chains of custody that mitigate greenwashing risks and strengthen compliance credibility.
3. Expansion of Scope 3 and Supply Chain Transparency Requirements
As organizations move toward full lifecycle emissions reporting, the need for granular, supplier-level data is increasing. Circular supply chain platforms enable accurate tracking of material origins, processing, and environmental impact.
Market Challenges: Fragmentation and Integration Complexity
Despite strong momentum, adoption is constrained by several challenges:
• Lack of standardized data formats and certification systems across regions
• Integration complexity with existing enterprise systems (ERP, PLM, SCM)
• Fragmented supply chains with multiple independent stakeholders
• Data accuracy and validation issues across multi-tier networks
These factors increase implementation costs and slow adoption, particularly for companies operating across diverse regulatory environments.
Emerging Opportunities: Platforms as Ecosystems and Transaction Engines
The next phase of growth lies in expanding platform functionality beyond traceability:
• Integrated marketplaces for sourcing and trading PCR materials
• Automated compliance reporting linked to regulatory frameworks
• AI-driven analytics for anomaly detection and supply chain optimization
• Financial integration, including sustainability-linked transactions and credits
