articles.title: After ruling in free speech case, Augusta considers new public comment policy
articles.author: Centralmaine.com
articles.content:
The Augusta Board of Education will soon consider approving a new public comment policy to align with a federal court ruling last week that held some parts of the board’s rules likely violate the First Amendment.
U.S. District Judge Stacey D. Neumann issued an injunction April 27 ordering the Augusta school board to stop enforcing rules aimed at limiting gossip and abusive or vulgar language during the public comment period of its meetings. Those rules are overly broad, Neumann wrote, and “impermissibly burden protected speech.”
Conservative activist Nicholas Blanchard sued the board earlier this year over those rules, saying he’d been unconstitutionally shut down by board chair Martha Witham. The litigation remains ongoing.
Blanchard is now running for an open seat on the board in a June 9 special election.
The board’s policy committee agreed Monday to present the rest of the board with a new, attorney-written policy that removes parts of the rules referenced by Neumann’s order — specifically, the rules that bar public comment speakers from discussing “gossip” and “abusive or vulgar language.”
Superintendent Michael Tracy said the district received advice from Drummond Woodsum, the legal firm that represents Augusta schools, to revise the policy as soon as possible following Neumann’s ruling.
The board will consider the revised rules in its meeting on Wednesday, May 13. Tracy said members could vote to waive further deliberation on the new policy and adopt it immediately.
“Keep in mind, if a federal district court has found parts of our current (public comment) policy — I don’t want to say unconstitutional — not be able to hold up against the Constitution or some of those First Amendment rights, that’s important that we address that,” Tracy said during Monday’s meeting.
The new policy also changes a rule barring discussion of “personal matters” to “personnel matters.” Neumann called out the original wording in her decision as unconstitutionally vague.
Witham said the original wording was likely an unintentional clerical error, and the goal of the policy was always to prevent comments about the job performance or conduct of specific district staff. “Personnel matters” are a common restriction in public comment policies.
Via a statement written by Drummond Woodsum attorney Melissa Hewey, Witham said in Monday’s meeting that the changes are intended to comply with Neumann’s ruling and remedy First Amendment concerns, while maintaining “decorum and civility” during meetings.
“We plan to revise our policy as necessary to ensure that it stands up to our commitment to the First Amendment while continuing to provide protection to the privacy of our students and employees that the law also requires,” the statement said.
“It is important to note that the court’s opinion was based on the language of our public comment policy, not on a specific treatment of Mr. Blanchard,” the statement continued. “We do not read the Court’s opinion as giving Mr. Blanchard or anyone else free reign to disrupt the business of the Board, and we are committed to conducting our meetings in a way that exemplifies civility and respect for all.”
Although the board plans to consider approving the revised policy at the May 13 meeting, the ordinary public comment period precedes the business portion of the meeting.
The current public comment policy will apply, and Witham, the board chair, will not be allowed to enforce the rules affected by the federal court decision.
articles.summary: The Augusta Board of Education will soon consider approving a new public comment policy to align with a federal court ruling last week that held some parts of the board’s rules likely violate the First Amendment. U.S. District Judge Stacey D. Neumann issued an injunction April 27 ordering the Augusta school board to stop enforcing rules aimed at limiting gossip and abusive or vulgar language during the public comment period of its meetings.

articles.title: SENER Makes Case for Fuel Subsidy Policy
articles.author: Mexico Business News
articles.content:
Luz Elena González Escobar addresses Mexico's IEPS-based price containment as a deliberate, structurally grounded policy response to what she describes as the most significant reshaping of the global energy order since the 1970s, and defends the fiscal cost of subsidies as a legitimate priority.
Energy Minister Luz Elena González Escobar laid out the government's economic and political rationale for its fuel price containment policy, characterizing the current global energy disruption as a moment of historic consequence and positioning Mexico's response as a model of institutional resilience. The addressing comes as Brent crude has surpassed the US$120/b threshold, the US average regular gasoline price has exceeded US$4.22 per gallon, and Mexico's weekly IEPS stimulus has oscillated between a partial offset and near-complete absorption of statutory fuel taxes.
González opens her column in El Financiero by framing the global context: "The world's energy order is changing; we may be witnessing the most important mutation since the 1970s." She identifies two simultaneous drivers: conflict-driven pressure on the Persian Gulf, the commercial route central to global oil and gas supply, and internal fractures within OPEC.
The Mexican Exception and Its Architecture
Against the backdrop of international volatility, González argues that Mexico stands out for its stability, having managed to maintain prices and supply forecasts in its energy market, particularly for gasoline and diesel, through a combination of responsible use of the IEPS subsidy mechanism, direct dialogue with the fuel retail sector, and measures to reduce operators' cost structures. The practical consequence, she notes, is that Mexican families have been shielded from the most severe effects of external price fluctuations.
She notes that without the government's intervention, gasoline prices in Mexico would have exceeded MX$30/L, a figure that aligns with President Sheinbaum's own statements and with the Ministry of Finance's weekly IEPS stimulus disclosures, which show the government absorbing between MX$3/L and MX$6/L in forgone fuel tax revenue depending on the week.
The minister places particular emphasis on diesel, noting that its price has a direct bearing on the cost of transporting all categories of goods, and therefore on food and basic consumer prices across the economy. The diesel price cap, she argues, is not a concession to the logistics sector but a direct protection for household purchasing power, and the government acted on that basis, in agreement with business operators and in a timely manner.
The Structural Foundations of Mexico's Resilience
González attributes the country's room for maneuver to a series of prior energy policy decisions, including the strengthening of the National Refining System, which has reduced Mexico's dependence on imported fuels and provided the country with greater tools for managing external shocks. She also cites the 2024 constitutional energy reform as a framework now yielding results through increased investment and development of national energy potential.
Diesel production rose 69.9% year-on-year in 1Q26 to 285.7Mb/d, and total oil product output increased 21.9% to 1.110MMb/d, according to IMCO's quarterly PEMEX analysis. These figures reflect the Olmeca refinery's expanding contribution to domestic supply. A Mexico that produces more of its own diesel is less exposed to the pass-through of international price spikes into domestic transport costs than it was four or five years ago.
The Fiscal Acknowledgment
The column is notable for its directness on the fiscal dimension of the policy, a point that the Finance Ministry and analysts at IMEF have raised in recent weeks. González acknowledges that the use of fiscal incentives implies a budgetary effort that must be managed with discipline and transparency, while arguing that in a context of high global volatility, the decision to absorb external shocks responds to a legitimate priority: protecting purchasing power, preserving economic stability, and safeguarding Mexican welfare.
The acknowledgment is measured but significant. IMEF analysts have warned that forgone IEPS revenue does not disappear from the fiscal accounting but effectively deferred to future years when higher fuel tax rates or lower spending must offset the current-year gap. Mexico spent approximately US$280 million per week in IEPS fuel subsidies at the height of the oil price spike in April, and the IEA has projected that prices will remain elevated through at least the third quarter of 2026 if the Strait of Hormuz does not fully reopen.
articles.summary: Luz Elena González Escobar addresses Mexico's IEPS-based price containment as a deliberate, structurally grounded policy response to what she describes as the most significant reshaping of the global energy order since the 1970s, and defends the fiscal cost of subsidies as a legitimate priority.

articles.title: Reading China's Next Chapter: Premia Partners on Policy Alignment, Hardcore Tech, and the Case for Precision Allocation
articles.author: Hubbis
articles.content:
Reading China's Next Chapter: Premia Partners on Policy Alignment, Hardcore Tech, and the Case for Precision Allocation
As the opening year of China's 15th Five-Year Plan reshapes the country's capital markets and sector hierarchy, investors across Asia are reassessing how to access an economy that looks fundamentally different from the platform-driven story of the past decade. At a recent Hubbis-hosted closed-door luncheon in Bangkok, Rebecca Chua, Managing Partner of Premia Partners, walked senior investment professionals through where she sees the most durable opportunities, why earnings growth has become the single most important signal in Chinese equities, and how Asia's broader innovation ecosystem fits into a more nuanced allocation framework.
Key Takeaways
- Policy Alignment as Alpha Engine: Sectors aligned with China's previous five-year plan delivered roughly 41 percent average return over the policy cycle, against minus three percent for the CSI 300, making the 15th Five-Year Plan a critical reference point for 2026 positioning.
- From Platform to Hardcore Tech: The performance leadership has shifted decisively from mega-cap internet platforms to semiconductors, robotics, advanced manufacturing, biotech and quantum technology, where earnings are accelerating rather than being absorbed into capital expenditure.
- Onshore Versus Offshore Divergence: Onshore China hardcore tech leaders have meaningfully outpaced offshore China strategies that focus on traditional internet and platform companies strategies year-to-date, reflecting where the new earnings power actually sits.
- Domestic Substitution at Scale: Chinese chipmakers are positioned to take significant GPU and memory chip market share previously held by foreign suppliers, supported by domestic substitution procurement mandates targeting electric vehicle, data centre and Internet of Things (IoT) manufacturers that distribute domestically.
- Taiwan and Korea as Complements: Beyond China, Taiwan and Korea offer access to the picks-and-shovels providers in the chip super cycle underpinning the global AI build-out, with the alpha increasingly sitting outside the most familiar mega-cap names.
- Geopolitical Risk Premium Is Now Universal: Strategic-sector deal scrutiny is no longer a China-specific issue but a feature investors need to be mindful of when allocating globally.
A Differentiated ETF House Built for Asia
Premia Partners is a Hong Kong-based exchange-traded fund (ETF) manager with twelve ETFs listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, spanning China, Taiwan, Vietnam, Asia innovation and emerging ASEAN, alongside five fixed income ETFs covering Chinese government bonds, US Treasuries, Saudi government sukuk and Asia ex-Japan investment-grade US dollar bonds. The firm's China STAR 50 ETF also has a depositary receipt listed on the Stock Exchange of Thailand in partnership with Bualuang Securities.
Chua framed the role of ETFs in a market moving as quickly as Chinese technology. "Even for the most successful active managers, it would be very difficult to already develop up to date research and a conviction basket quickly," she said, noting that ETFs increasingly serve as convenient placeholders that allow allocators to express a thematic view by a one ticker trade, without being "wedded to the idea for life" in the way mutual funds or mandates require.
Why Onshore China Has Decoupled from Offshore Sentiment
A recurring theme in Chua's diagnosis was the gap between investor perceptions shaped by Hong Kong-listed proxies and the reality unfolding onshore. Many Thai allocators, she observed, still equate "China tech" with offshore China focused Hang Seng Tech, the Hang Seng Index, or KWEB, all of which have been weak year-to-date. By contrast, the CSI 300 has posted a positive return in the mid-single digits, and Premia Partners' STAR 50 ETF is up roughly 12 percent year-to-date, with one-year performance above 50 percent.
The divergence reflects a structural shift in who is earning from the AI build-out. The familiar mega-cap internet names are spenders in this cycle, deploying significant capital expenditure to build AI infrastructure but yet to fully monetise it. China's overall AI capex is estimated at roughly 10 percent of the figure projected for the United States this year, a function of chip-ban restrictions that have forced domestic players to "do more with less," as Chua put it. The earners, meanwhile, are sitting in the hardware layer, what she described as "the choke point economics."
Hardcore Technology and the STAR Market
The Shanghai STAR Market, established in 2019, was designed to incubate domestic champions in hardcore technology, and its top constituents now include leading Chinese chipmakers across GPU, memory, specialty semiconductor segments and physical AI in the form of humanoid and industrial robotics. Procurement mandates instructing local data centre operators, electric vehicle manufacturers and IoT players to raise their domestic content have translated into accelerating earnings for these firms. Cambricon, one of the leading Chinese AI chip companies, broke even in the fourth quarter of 2025 and reported its first full year of profit, with 2026 expected to be a strongly positive year on the back of policy support and major customer wins, Chua noted.
She pointed to a Bernstein analysis which projected that Nvidia's GPU market share in China could fall from 54 percent last year to roughly 8 percent this year, with the displaced share absorbed by domestic substitutes. On the memory side, emerging Chinese players are positioned to gradually replace high-end AI memory imports, although industry consensus expects the global memory cycle to remain tight through 2028.
Robotics, Renewables and the Industrial Use Case
Beyond semiconductors, Chua highlighted physical AI in the form of robotics as a second leg of the hardcore-tech thesis, with the critical caveat that monetisation rather than spectacle is now what drives institutional flows. "More investor interest would be on those AI players, chipmakers, and robotic leaders that have more robust use partners so that they would be able to monetise and also have more credible use cases rather than just for show," she said.
She also flagged renewable energy as a category being re-rated through an AI lens. Solar manufacturers, energy storage system (ESS) providers and components suppliers, including the Thailand-listed Delta Electronics that leads in the power management system for AI server and data centre space, are increasingly viewed as part of the AI infrastructure ecosystem rather than traditional industrial, utility-adjacent plays, given their role in powering data centres.
The 15th Five-Year Plan as Structural Reference
Chua urged the audience to read the language of the 15th Five-Year Plan closely, given the historical pattern of sector outperformance for plan-aligned industries. AI, aerospace and quantum technology remain core focus areas, with quantum names beginning to appear within the STAR 50 index. Biotech also features, although she stressed an important distinction: the Hang Seng Tech biotech cohort is concentrated in contract manufacturing organisations exposed to US Biosecure Act risk, while the onshore biotech beneficiaries are innovative drug developers benefiting from the global patent cliff. Chinese licensing-out revenue reached USD138 billion last year, with global pharmaceutical companies paying significant upfront and ongoing fees to access Chinese pipelines in oncology, antibody-drug conjugates and weight-loss therapeutics.
Earnings Growth as the Decisive Signal
Across sectors, Chua returned repeatedly to a single discipline. "Earnings growth is the number one signal for the best performing Chinese company this year because investors increasingly are less satisfied with just talks," she said. "If you have a story, it's good to catch their attention maybe for a few weeks, but people would quickly divert their attention to those that can really deliver and monetise."
International flows, she noted, have not fully returned to peak allocation levels but have increasingly concentrated in onshore names rather than offshore proxies, with European and Middle Eastern investors particularly active in chipmaker and robotics due diligence.
Beyond China: Taiwan and Asia Innovation
Chua argued that many investors are over-concentrated in TSMC as their Taiwan exposure, missing the alpha generated by the upstream materials and component providers. The premium of TSMC's American depositary receipts has recently compressed from around 30 percent historically to roughly 17 percent, reflecting broader investor interest in the wider Taiwan ecosystem. Taiwan now carries the largest weighting in the MSCI Emerging Markets Index at roughly 21 percent, just ahead of China at around 19 to 20 percent and becomes also one of the largest equity markets globally with market capitalization ahead of the UK and Canada.
For investors looking to capture the regional AI build-out more broadly, Chua flagged Premia Partners' Asia Innovative Technology ETF as her personal high-conviction pick, citing the strength of Korean equities, which were up almost 80 percent last year and a further 50 percent year-to-date.
Implications for Allocators
For wealth managers and allocators in the region, the practical message is one of precision. Broad China exposures and familiar offshore proxies are unlikely to capture where earnings are actually compounding. Instead, allocators willing to align with policy direction, focus on monetisation rather than narrative, and broaden their lens beyond the most liquid mega-caps stand to benefit most as the 15th Five-Year Plan cycle unfolds.
As Chua summarised, the year ahead will be volatile, "but there will always be people that make money in this kind of market especially those that are able to rotate and ETFs are great access tools for such. "
More from Rebecca Chua, Premia Partners

articles.summary: Reading China's Next Chapter: Premia Partners on Policy Alignment, Hardcore Tech, and the Case for Precision Allocation As the opening year of China's 15th Five-Year Plan reshapes the country's capital markets and sector hierarchy, investors across Asia are reassessing how to access an economy that looks fundamentally different from the platform-driven story of the past decade.

articles.title: Industrial policy now has broad World Bank approval but the case for universal adoption remains unclear | Mint
articles.author: Mint
articles.content:
Dennis Robertson was not only one of the finest economic minds of the 20th century, but also an elegant writer who was known for his witticisms. In an essay written in 1956, Robertson quipped: “High-brow opinion is like a hunted hare; if you stand in the same place, or nearly the same place, it can be relied upon to come round to you in a circle.”
Those words resonate while reading a new report by the World Bank on industrial policy, or targeted government intervention to shape the economic structure of a country by promoting, protecting or developing specific industries deemed vital to economic growth, export competitiveness, import substitution or geopolitical strategy.
In simpler terms, the government has a say in what is produced within a country. The multilateral lender had famously released a report in 1993 on the miracle economies of East Asia, where it had said that the main reasons for success stories in the region were sound macroeconomic management, investment in human capital and productivity growth driven by export industries. Industrial policy to aid specific sectors or companies was less important in comparison.
Cut to 2026. World Bank chief economist Indermit Gill wrote in the foreword to its new report that the earlier injunction against industrial policy “has not aged well—it has the practical value of a floppy disk today.”
In 2019, economists at the International Monetary Fund had a witty title for a paper that described industrial policy as ‘the policy that shall not be named.’ Be it the analogy of the hunted hare, the floppy disk or Lord Voldemort of Harry Potter novels, it is clear that the pendulum has swung back towards industrial policy.
At the heart of the new framework is a set of three country characteristics that the report argues are decisive in determining what kind of industrial policy is feasible. These are: government capacity for sustained interaction with multiple businesses and industries; local market size to achieve economies of scale; and fiscal space to bear the costs of business subsidies without sacrificing spending on social services.
Interestingly, the World Bank says that India scores well on all three, which implicitly means it has the requisite means to pursue industrial policy.
This is a useful taxonomy. It does what good policy frameworks are supposed to do: it converts an ideological debate into a diagnostic one. The question is no longer whether industrial policy is virtuous or vicious in the abstract, but whether a particular government in a particular country at a particular moment has the three things it needs to make a particular tool work.
These three traits determine which of 15 possible industrial policy tools will work best—ranging from industrial parks and job-skills training all the way to import tariffs, production subsidies and competitive exchange-rate devaluations. These tools are a mix of sharp and blunt instruments, and their effectiveness depends on progressively higher levels of market size, government capacity and fiscal space.
In the case of India, there is a lot of attention paid to industrial policy at the sub-national level, especially in Tamil Nadu. The World Bank has paid special attention to how the state succeeded in attracting production of Apple’s iPhone 16 through a combination of what it describes as a top-down and bottom-up approach.
The former includes subsidies for specific industries, while the latter covers specific coordination failures such as lack of housing for workers. It built housing for 18,000 workers near the factory site even before the production facility came up, something that a private builder may not have invested in without guarantees of adequate rental returns.
One salient fact about industrial policy in our times is that most governments seem to have some variant of it. The World Bank reports that all 183 member countries target at least one industry. There are some noteworthy patterns here. For example, poor countries often depend on blunt instruments such as higher tariffs to promote domestic production, while upper-middle-income countries are big spenders on business subsidies.
However, Gill warns in a recent blog on the World Bank website: “By itself, industrial policy has seldom been a game-changer: the record shows that, even under ideal conditions (emphasis added), it results in an average gain of just 1% of [gross domestic product]. Still, in an era of persistently sluggish growth, every option to boost growth ought to be considered.”
The report’s most important omission is this: Can all 183 countries pursue an industrial policy simultaneously?
It is akin to a mutual depreciation problem in foreign-exchange markets. It is logically impossible for all countries to depreciate their currencies together. Just as all countries cannot run trade surpluses. Does something similar apply to industrial policy?
The East Asian success stories had something that no framework can manufacture on demand: they were exporting into a global economy that was broadly open and not itself engaged in the same game.
South Korea’s shipbuilding and semiconductor industries were subsidized at home and targeted markets overseas that, whatever their imperfections, were not simultaneously running competing subsidy programmes of comparable scale. It is hard to believe, for example, that all major economies can achieve economies of scale—and hence efficiency—in semiconductors for domestic use.
In other words, is the very ubiquity of industrial policy in our times also a barrier to its eventual success?
The author is executive director at Artha India Research Advisors.

articles.title: Vehicle Transfer Case Market in the United States | Report - IndexBox - Prices, Size, Forecast, and Companies
articles.author: IndexBox
articles.content:
AutoZone Q2 Fiscal 2026 Earnings Beat Estimates, Revenue Misses
AutoZone's Q2 fiscal 2026 earnings surpassed analyst expectations at $27.63 per share, though revenue of $4.27 billion was slightly below forecasts.
The United States Vehicle Transfer Case market encompasses the design, production, distribution, and aftermarket servicing of driveline components that distribute torque from the transmission to both front and rear axles in four-wheel drive (4WD) and all-wheel drive (AWD) vehicles. As a tangible, engineered automotive subsystem, the transfer case sits at the intersection of mechanical power transmission and increasingly sophisticated electronic control systems. The market serves a vehicle parc that is heavily skewed toward light trucks, SUVs, and crossovers—segments that together represent approximately 78% of new vehicle registrations in the United States as of 2025–2026.
The product category spans three primary technology architectures: gear-driven units (both part-time and full-time), chain-driven units, and electro-mechanical active on-demand systems. A fourth, emerging segment—integrated torque-vectoring transfer cases—is gaining traction in performance-oriented and luxury platforms. The market is further segmented by value chain position, with OEM-fitted units representing roughly 70–75% of total market value, aftermarket replacement and remanufactured units accounting for 18–22%, and service/rebuild kits making up the remainder. The United States functions as both a high-cost engineering and niche manufacturing hub for transfer cases, while also serving as the world's largest single-country demand market for these components.
The United States Vehicle Transfer Case market is estimated at USD 4.8–5.3 billion in 2026, inclusive of OEM program pricing, Tier-1 integrator transfer prices, aftermarket list prices, and remanufactured unit sales. This valuation reflects the aggregate value of transfer cases sold as original equipment on domestically produced vehicles, imported units fitted to foreign-built vehicles sold in the US, and all aftermarket transactions including service kits. The market has grown at a compound annual rate of approximately 3.5–4.0% from 2020 to 2026, closely tracking the expansion of the US light-truck and SUV parc.
Volume terms indicate roughly 6.2–6.8 million transfer case units (new and remanufactured) entering the US market annually in 2026, including both OEM installations and aftermarket sales. The average unit value across all channels is estimated at USD 720–820, with significant variance by technology type: gear-driven units average USD 450–600, chain-driven units USD 550–700, and electro-mechanical active on-demand units USD 900–1,300. The aftermarket average unit price is lower, typically USD 350–550 for remanufactured units and USD 600–900 for new OE-replacement units. Growth through 2035 is projected at a CAGR of 3.0–3.8%, driven by rising 4WD/AWD penetration rates, increasing vehicle longevity, and technology content escalation in new platforms.
Light-duty trucks and SUVs constitute the dominant demand segment, accounting for approximately 68–72% of transfer case volume in the United States. This includes full-size pickups (Ford F-Series, Ram, Chevrolet Silverado), mid-size pickups, and body-on-frame SUVs, which predominantly use gear-driven or chain-driven transfer cases with part-time or full-time 4WD systems. Crossover and unibody SUV platforms, which increasingly employ electro-mechanical on-demand transfer cases, represent the fastest-growing application segment, expanding at 5–7% annually as consumers migrate from sedans to AWD crossovers.
Heavy-duty and commercial off-highway applications—including Class 4–8 trucks, delivery vans, agricultural equipment, and construction machinery—account for 12–15% of unit demand. These applications require ruggedized, high-torque-capacity transfer cases, often with integrated PTO (power take-off) provisions. Performance and luxury vehicles, including high-end SUVs and sports cars with AWD systems, represent 6–9% of volume but command disproportionate value due to advanced torque-vectoring and electro-hydraulic control features.
Military and special-purpose vehicles, while smaller in volume at 2–4%, involve specialized procurement programs with extended lifecycle support requirements and premium pricing structures. End-use sectors are dominated by passenger vehicles (SUV/crossover/pickup) at roughly 80% of demand, with light commercial vehicles at 12%, off-highway and agricultural equipment at 5%, and defense and government fleets at 3%.
Pricing in the United States Vehicle Transfer Case market operates across distinct layers, each with its own cost structure and margin profile. OEM program pricing is established per vehicle platform over 5–10 year lifecycles, typically ranging from USD 400–800 per unit for mainstream light-truck applications and USD 900–1,500 for premium electro-mechanical systems. Tier-1 integrator transfer prices—the price at which a transfer case manufacturer sells to a transmission or driveline integrator—add 15–25% to the component cost base. Aftermarket list prices for OE-replacement units range from USD 600–1,200, while competitive replacement brands price 20–35% below OE equivalents.
Key cost drivers include raw material exposure to aluminum, steel, and specialty alloys; precision gear cutting and honing operations that require high capital investment; and electronic component costs for sensor suites, solenoids, and control modules in active systems. Forged gear sets and specialty bearings represent 25–35% of total material cost and are subject to long lead times and concentrated supply. Labor costs in US-based manufacturing facilities are a significant factor, with domestic production carrying an estimated 40–60% labor cost premium versus low-cost sourcing hubs.
Remanufactured unit pricing is typically 40–60% below new OE equivalents, with exchange program prices ranging from USD 350–600 depending on core condition and technology complexity. Service and overhaul kits—containing seals, bearings, clutch packs, and gaskets—are priced at USD 80–250 and represent a high-margin consumable segment.
The competitive landscape in the United States Vehicle Transfer Case market is characterized by a mix of integrated Tier-1 system suppliers, specialist transfer case and 4WD technology manufacturers, OEM-captive component divisions, and aftermarket specialists. The market is moderately concentrated, with the top five suppliers estimated to account for 55–65% of OEM-fitted unit volume. Key participants include global driveline system integrators such as Dana Incorporated, American Axle & Manufacturing (AAM), and Magna International (through its Magna Powertrain division), each of which operates engineering and production facilities in the United States. BorgWarner is a significant technology leader in electro-mechanical and torque-vectoring transfer cases, supplying multiple US and foreign OEM platforms.
Specialist manufacturers, including Marmon-Herrington and Fabco Automotive Corporation, serve niche segments such as heavy-duty commercial, military, and custom off-road applications. OEM-captive divisions, notably within the Detroit driveline operations of major truck manufacturers, produce transfer cases for captive vehicle platforms. The aftermarket competitive arena includes recognized rebuilders and distributors such as Cardone Industries, ACDelco, and TransTec, alongside numerous regional remanufacturers. Competition centers on durability, NVH (noise/vibration/harshness) performance, weight reduction, and electronic control sophistication, with technology differentiation increasingly driven by software and calibration expertise rather than purely mechanical design.
The United States maintains a meaningful but not dominant domestic production base for vehicle transfer cases, with estimated annual production capacity of 3.2–3.8 million units across facilities in Michigan, Ohio, Indiana, New York, and the Carolinas. Domestic production is concentrated on high-value, complex assemblies—particularly electro-mechanical and torque-vectoring units—where engineering proximity to OEM customers and intellectual property protection justify higher manufacturing costs. Several facilities operate as "customer-facing" assembly and test centers, performing final assembly, calibration, and validation while sourcing precision-machined components from domestic and international suppliers.
Production constraints include the high capital intensity of precision gear cutting and honing lines, which require USD 15–25 million in investment per production cell, and the limited availability of skilled machinists and manufacturing engineers. Domestic forging capacity for transfer case gear sets is particularly constrained, with only a handful of specialized suppliers capable of meeting OEM quality and volume requirements. The United States also hosts significant remanufacturing operations, with an estimated 150–200 facilities—ranging from large national rebuilders to small regional shops—processing 1.0–1.4 million transfer case cores annually. Core availability, quality consistency, and the increasing electronic complexity of late-model units present ongoing supply challenges for the remanufacturing sector.
The United States is a net importer of vehicle transfer cases and their component subassemblies, with imports estimated at USD 2.8–3.3 billion in 2026 against exports of USD 1.0–1.3 billion. The primary HS codes covering these products—870840 (gear boxes and parts thereof) and 870899 (other parts and accessories for motor vehicles)—capture the majority of transfer case trade flows, though exact attribution is complicated by the inclusion of these components within broader driveline assemblies. Major import sources include Mexico, where US-owned and foreign-owned Tier-1 suppliers operate high-volume assembly plants serving the NAFTA/USMCA production corridor; Japan, supplying transfer cases for Japanese-brand vehicles assembled in North America; and Germany, providing premium electro-mechanical units for European luxury brands sold in the US.
Import dependence is structurally driven by the concentration of high-volume transfer case production in low-cost and proximity-sourcing locations, with Mexico alone accounting for an estimated 35–45% of US import value. China supplies a growing share of aftermarket replacement units and component subassemblies, though at lower average unit values. Tariff treatment under USMCA provides duty-free access for Mexican and Canadian-origin transfer cases meeting regional value content rules, while imports from other origins face most-favored-nation rates typically in the 2.5–4.0% range.
Export flows are dominated by high-value electro-mechanical and torque-vectoring units shipped to European and Asian vehicle platforms, as well as aftermarket units destined for Canada, Latin America, and the Middle East. Trade policy developments, including potential tariff adjustments and USMCA review, represent a material uncertainty for supply chain configuration.
Distribution in the United States Vehicle Transfer Case market follows distinct pathways for OEM and aftermarket channels. OEM-fitted units are delivered through direct contractual relationships between transfer case manufacturers and vehicle OEMs or Tier-1 driveline integrators, with procurement managed by OEM drivetrain engineering and purchasing departments. These relationships involve multi-year program awards, just-in-time delivery schedules, and extensive collaborative engineering during the vehicle platform definition and architecture phase. Buyer groups in this channel include OEM drivetrain engineering teams, Tier-1 transmission and driveline integrators, and, for military and special-purpose variants, government procurement agencies and large fleet operators.
The aftermarket distribution channel is more fragmented, encompassing national and regional aftermarket distributors (such as NAPA, O'Reilly Auto Parts, and AutoZone), warehouse distributors specializing in driveline components, and direct sales to independent repair shops and fleet maintenance facilities. Aftermarket buyers include national and regional aftermarket distributors, large fleet operators, specialist off-road and performance upfitters, and independent service centers. Remanufactured and exchange-program units flow primarily through warehouse distributors and program groups, with core return logistics managed by rebuilders.
Service and rebuild kits are distributed through similar channels, with additional penetration through online marketplaces and e-commerce platforms serving DIY enthusiasts and small repair shops. The workflow stages from vehicle platform definition through aftermarket distribution create multiple touchpoints for suppliers, with engineering and validation services increasingly offered as a value-add alongside component supply.
Vehicle transfer cases sold in the United States are subject to a regulatory framework that influences design, material selection, and performance validation. Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS) govern the safety of AWD system controls, particularly regarding unintended torque application and vehicle stability. Compliance with FMVSS 126 (Electronic Stability Control) and FMVSS 135 (Light Vehicle Brake Systems) imposes requirements on transfer case control logic and integration with vehicle dynamics systems.
Emissions regulations under EPA and CARB authority indirectly drive transfer case design through parasitic loss reduction requirements, as driveline efficiency directly affects fuel economy and CO2 compliance. The Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards and EPA greenhouse gas regulations create pressure for lightweight materials and low-friction designs, with transfer case weight reductions of 1–3 kg per unit contributing to fleet-level compliance.
End-of-Life Vehicle (ELV) directives, while primarily European in origin, influence material choices for US-market vehicles as global platforms adopt common design standards. This drives adoption of recyclable aluminum alloys and restricts use of certain hazardous substances in seals, gaskets, and electronic components. Homologation requirements for off-road and military variants involve additional testing for water fording, extreme temperature operation, and durability under sustained high-torque loads.
For aftermarket units, compliance with EPA's aftermarket parts regulations and state-level emissions warranty requirements affects the sale of replacement transfer cases, particularly for OBD-II equipped vehicles where proper communication with the vehicle's electronic control network must be maintained. The regulatory landscape is evolving toward greater scrutiny of electronic driveline controls as vehicles become more software-defined, with potential implications for cybersecurity certification and over-the-air update capabilities in future transfer case designs.
The United States Vehicle Transfer Case market is forecast to grow from USD 4.8–5.3 billion in 2026 to USD 6.5–7.5 billion by 2035, representing a compound annual growth rate of 3.0–3.8%. Volume growth is expected to moderate as vehicle electrification reduces the total number of transfer cases required for battery-electric platforms, though this effect will be partially offset by continued strong demand for internal combustion and hybrid 4WD/AWD vehicles through the early 2030s. The electro-mechanical and active on-demand segment is projected to become the largest technology type by value by 2032, surpassing gear-driven units, as platform modularity strategies enable 2WD/AWD flexibility on shared architectures.
Aftermarket demand is forecast to grow at 3.5–4.5% annually, outpacing OEM growth, driven by the aging vehicle parc and increasing complexity of replacement units. The remanufactured segment will benefit from growing core availability as 2020–2025 model-year vehicles enter the replacement cycle. Lightweight material adoption is expected to accelerate, with aluminum and magnesium composite housings becoming standard on over 60% of new OEM transfer case programs by 2030.
Integrated torque-vectoring transfer cases, while currently a premium niche, are forecast to expand into mid-market SUV platforms, adding USD 200–350 in incremental value per unit. The military and special-purpose vehicle segment is projected to see stable demand, with potential upside from defense modernization programs and replacement cycles for the US military's light tactical vehicle fleet. Overall, the market's value growth will increasingly be driven by technology content escalation rather than pure volume expansion, as each new generation of transfer case incorporates more electronics, software, and precision engineering.
Significant opportunities exist in the United States Vehicle Transfer Case market for suppliers and technology developers positioned to address the shift toward electrified and software-defined drivelines. The transition to hybrid and plug-in hybrid electric vehicle platforms creates demand for compact, lightweight transfer cases capable of integrating with electric drive units and managing torque split between internal combustion and electric propulsion sources. Suppliers that develop transfer case designs optimized for hybrid architectures—with reduced parasitic losses, integrated thermal management, and seamless mode transitions—are well-positioned to capture program awards as OEMs expand their electrified SUV and light-truck offerings.
The aftermarket presents a substantial opportunity for remanufacturers and distributors capable of addressing the growing complexity of electro-mechanical transfer cases. articles.title: Arizona's criminal case against Kalshi permanently blocked by federal judge | Arizona Mirror
articles.author: Arizona Mirror
articles.content:
11:34
Brief
A federal judge has permanently blocked Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes from prosecuting Kalshi, halting the state’s unprecedented attempt to criminally charge an online prediction market company with violating state gambling laws.
Even though regulating gambling is “among the most rudimentary exercises of state police power,” Judge Michael Liburdi concluded that federal law preempts the state from enforcing those laws against Kalshi and other prediction market companies because they are exclusively regulated by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.
“Every time Congress has revisited the federal-state allocation of authority in this area, it has chosen to expand federal control,” Liburdi wrote in an order granting a preliminary injunction that the CFTC sought. “It has done so while expressing unease about the costs of state-by-state regulation.”
GET THE MORNING HEADLINES.
In March, Mayes announced she had indicted Kalshi with 20 misdemeanors. She alleged the firm broke Arizona law prohibiting the operation of an unlicensed wagering business and similarly broke the law by allowing bets on Arizona elections.
The New York-based company has been center stage in an ongoing battle over how to regulate prediction markets, which allow for bets on a variety of topics, from sports to politics to the war in Iran. The prediction markets have also been accused of insider trading, as unknown people have made large sums of money off real world events.
In 2024, Kalshi won a landmark case in federal court when the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit ruled that the Commodity Futures Trading Commission couldn’t block its election wagering under federal law. As a result, the company now operates as a “designated contract market” that is regulated by the CFTC.
Mayes argued that Kalshi’s authority to operate under federal law doesn’t preempt Arizona’s criminal laws, setting up a federalism clash that could reverberate nationwide, as more than a dozen states similarly outlaw gambling on elections.
But Liburdi said the congressional record is clear that Kalshi and other prediction market companies are solely regulated by the CFTC, and that trumps the state gambling laws in Arizona and elsewhere. Were that not the case, he said, there it would be impossible for those businesses to comply with 50 different regulators.
“The result would be the inconsistent regulatory patchwork that Congress intended to avoid. Because Arizona’s gambling laws stand as an obstacle to federal regulation, those laws are preempted,” he wrote.
In granting the preliminary injunction, Liburdi turned an earlier temporary restraining order issued in mid-April into a permanent end to the state’s prosecution of Kalshi.
It’s unclear whether the state will appeal the order; a spokesman for Mayes said the Attorney General’s Office “continues to evaluate our legal options related to the case” but hasn’t decided its next steps.

articles.title: Days on Market Is Not a Scarlet Letter: The Case for Keeping Real Estate’s Most Misread Metric
articles.author: StreetInsider
articles.content:
Days on Market Is Not a Scarlet Letter: The Case for Keeping Real Estate’s Most Misread Metric
There is a quiet campaign underway in parts of the American real estate industry to make days on market disappear. Some brokerages and industry voices argue that displaying how long a listing has been active puts sellers at a disadvantage, giving buyers a negotiation lever without requiring them to disclose anything equivalent about themselves. It sounds reasonable. But a growing number of practitioners say it is the wrong approach.
Mark Gordon, co-owner of Christiania Realty in Vail, Colorado (vailcoluxuryhomes.com), has spent nearly two decades in a market where inventory is scarce and price points are high. He sees the push to hide days on market as part of a broader and more concerning trend: the erosion of the transparent marketplace that makes real estate transactions work for everyone.
The Argument Against Transparency
The case for removing DOM from public view goes something like this: a seller’s listing accumulates days, and each day that passes signals weakness. Buyers see 90 days on market and assume there is a problem with the property, the price, or both. They make lower offers. The seller loses leverage. Meanwhile, the buyer discloses almost nothing: not how many offers they have made elsewhere, not how motivated they are, not how qualified. The information gap, so the argument goes, is unfair.
This argument is connected to a wider debate about private listings, pocket listings, and the role of the MLS – discussions that intersect with brokerage consolidation, data ownership, and the question of who real estate data ultimately serves.
Why Removing Data Creates Friction, Not Advantage
Gordon’s counter is direct. Market data, he argues, is what makes transactions happen. Remove it, and you create obstacles. “Knowledge, data, is the lubricant that creates transactions,” he says. “Every time we remove that lubricant, what we’re doing is creating metal-on-metal friction and creating roadblocks that keep a transaction from occurring.”
His argument rests on a practical reality. In a world of AI-powered data tools, days on market is easy to calculate. Even if the MLS stopped displaying it, any competent search algorithm would reconstruct it from listing dates. The metric is not going away. The only question is whether it sits inside the official system, where it is standardized and accurate, or gets reassembled outside of it, where it may not be.
But the more interesting part of Gordon’s position is his reframe of what the metric actually signals.
A High DOM Is Not a Failure. It Is an Invitation.
Gordon says he has worked with buyers who specifically search by days on market, looking for listings that others have passed over. Those buyers may start with a low offer. But a low offer is not the same as a final offer – and it opens a conversation that would not otherwise exist.
“A lowball offer is a million times better than no offer,” he says. “At least now we have a starting point. We have the ability to create something.”
This flips the conventional narrative. Rather than viewing accumulated DOM as damage, Gordon treats it as a filter that attracts a specific kind of buyer – one who is looking for perceived value and is willing to engage. If the seller counters well, the high DOM becomes an advantage, not a liability, because it brought the buyer to the table in the first place.
The Seller’s Real Enemy Is Not Data. It Is Silence.
The instinct to remove DOM reflects a broader pattern in real estate: the belief that controlling information protects clients. Gordon argues the opposite. A seller whose listing has been on the market for three months does not benefit from hiding that fact. They benefit from a skilled agent who can use the situation to generate conversations.
Being offended by a low offer, Gordon says, is a strategic mistake. Rather than viewing it as an insult, he encourages sellers to see it as engagement. “Instead of being insulted and upset by a so-called lowball offer, we should be thanking them because they took the time to offer to buy your home,” he says. He is clear that this does not mean accepting below-market prices – but it does mean staying in the conversation.
Engagement is the resource. Data is what creates it. And in a market where only 127 listings serve an entire mountain resort community, every data point that brings a buyer to the table has value.
What This Means for the Industry
The days-on-market debate is, at its core, a proxy fight about something larger: whether the real estate industry’s future is built on more transparency or less. The answer will shape how MLS systems operate, how brokerages compete for listings, and how consumers trust the process.
For buyers, the takeaway is practical: a high DOM does not mean a bad property. It may mean an opportunity that other buyers overlooked or a price that has not yet found its market. For sellers, the takeaway is similar: transparency is not the enemy. Silence is.
Mark Gordon is co-owner of Christiania Realty and a luxury real estate broker in Vail, Colorado, with deep roots in community advocacy, industry leadership, and mountain market expertise. Learn more at vailcoluxuryhomes.com or connect on LinkedIn.

articles.title: Swaps or bets? High court digs into sports prediction market case
articles.author: WWLP
articles.content:
BOSTON (SHNS) – Supreme Judicial Court judges queried attorneys Monday whether Kalshi’s sports-event contracts are swaps or bets, a key point in the case determining whether the popular prediction market can continue making those offerings available in Massachusetts.
“The definition of swap is pretty broad so tell me why it hasn’t preempted state law,” Justice Dalila Argaez Wendlandt said seconds after an attorney representing the commonwealth began testifying. “First, let’s start with are these things swaps?”
The case before the high court concerns whether a Superior Court judge erred in banning Kalshi, one of the largest prediction markets in the country, from taking action on sports-related events in Massachusetts.
In a brief presented to the court, attorneys for Kalshi argued the company’s sports-event contracts are considered swaps that are subject to the federal Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s (CFTC) “exclusive jurisdiction” on designated contract markets, or DCM, and preempt state regulations. Attorney General Andrea Campbell disagrees and says the company is essentially offering sports wagering without a state license.
The Commodity Exchange Commission defines a swap to include any agreement, contract or transaction that deals with any purchase, sale, payment, delivery or transaction “that is dependent on the occurrence, non-occurrence, or the extent of the occurrence of an event or contingency associated with a potential financial, economic, or commercial consequence.”
Justices appeared confused with a point Grant Mainland, an attorney appearing on behalf of Kalshi, made that Kalshi’s offerings deal with financial, economic or commercial consequences because people and companies have business tied up in sports.
“I had trouble following the potential financial, economic or commercial consequence here, because it’s a bet on a bet,” Justice Scott Kafker said.
On the other hand, Gerard Cedrone, the deputy state solicitor who represented the state Monday, said Kalshi’s offerings are not swaps and should be regulated by the state. That’s because Kalshi’s sports contracts don’t meet the criteria of dealing with an occurrence or nonoccurence of an event and potential financial consequences, he argued.
Wendlandt questioned this. She asked if there would be no payout on a hypothetical bet she makes on whether the Bruins win or lose.
Cedrone said no. He said the term event is more likely referencing the game itself – not whether someone scores or if a team wins or loses. And even if those instances are considered an event, they don’t have the type of financial consequences needed to be considered a swap.
Justices also pressed Mainland on how what Kalshi offers is different from a bet or a wager.
Mainland said they are “fundamentally different.” When a bettor goes to a casino or uses a sportsbook, he said, they are engaging in a bilateral transaction. The casino or sportsbook sets odds and pricing, and usually the bettor is going to be on the losing side. That’s “completely different” from derivative transactions, he said.
“I mean, for someone who wants to bet on a game, this is a way of betting on a game,” Kafker said, challenging Mainland’s point.
Cedrone disputed Kalshi’s stance that it’s different from a traditional betting operation. He said the Superior Court found that Kalshi has an affiliated entity that places bets on its platform. Sometimes another bettor will be on the other side of a bet, but often it’s Kalshi’s affiliated entity.
“They don’t set odds, they operate this marketplace where users can create these contracts with each other. The prices can change dynamically, so users can sell positions before the event resolves itself,” said Justice Serge Georges. “So, doesn’t that really resemble more of a financial exchange rather than a house based system?”
Cedrone acknowledged that in certain instances it may resemble a financial transaction. But it also resembles many forms of traditional sports betting, like bets placed on horse racing. Those bets involve parimutuel wagering where the racetrack is not acting as the house, individual bets are pooled, the racetrack gets a cut and bets are paid out to everyone. Notably, the racetrack doesn’t set the odds, those fluctuate based on how the money comes in.
“So, I just keep coming back to the point that it’s true that there may be distinctions between specific bets on Kalshi and specific types of sports betting and casinos,” Cedrone said. “But when you look at the whole picture, it is not able to draw a consistent, meaningful and principled distinction between the bets that it offers, and the bets that casinos offer.”
Justice Bessie Dewar pressed Cedrone on whether or how all 50 states could regulate Kalshi if it is overseen at the federal level.
“Doesn’t it make sense that something that’s on a DCM, which is this federally CFTC-regulated market, that it would be really unwieldy for 50 different states laws to be applicable to those transactions?” Dewar said.
Cedrone said that, in many areas, the Commodity Exchange Act leaves room for state regulations and that has been the norm for sports betting in the U.S.
Kafker also said that if Congress was making a major policy decision – like shifting oversight of sports gambling to the CFTC as Mainland says it did – it would do so more clearly.
Mainland noted that Congress was aware that event contracts may involve gaming when it passed a sweeping law in 2010 that overhauled U.S. financial regulation and authorized the CFTC to oversee the swaps market.
“That’s the only thing that distinguishes these derivatives is that the underlying event happens to be a sports event,” he said.
Kafker pushed back, saying gambling is something that states have traditionally regulated.
“I just feel like you’re swimming upstream,” he told Mainland.
Kalshi is involved in disputes with state regulators across the country over whether it should operate under state or federal laws. The prediction market operator is part of more than 30 cases. Massachusetts was the first state to sue Kalshi when Campbell filed the lawsuit in September.
The outcome of the case could likely set a precedent for how the surging and evolving prediction markets are regulated in the U.S.
